messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Lukas, a 21-year-old single bus driver of European background, came to treatment after months of feeling as though the war had never really ended for him. He had served in the military, and the event that still dominated his mind was a convoy incident overseas: a sudden bang that split the air, the sharp smell of something burnt, and the roar of helicopters overhead while everything around him seemed to fracture into urgency and confusion. When he tries to tell it, he does so in pieces. He knows what happened, but the story will not come out in a straight line; he reaches for words and cannot find them, as if the event has been broken into disconnected fragments that do not fit together. What remains is the film-like quality of it, with the same moments replaying without his permission—the sound, the smell, the sense that he is bracing for the next strike even when nothing is happening.

Since that time, Lukas has come to believe that the world is dangerous and that he has to be on guard all the time. That belief has shaped the way he moves through ordinary life. He avoids crowded places such as shopping centres or public events because he cannot shake the sense that in a crowd he would not notice danger in time. He also stays away from religious spaces and gatherings, though he does not speak about that easily; he says the quiet, enclosed atmosphere makes him feel cornered and exposed. More often, he retreats into long hours on his phone, games, or the internet, because distraction is the only thing that reliably keeps the images and sensations from taking over. He knows this is not helping, but the hours disappear quickly, and for a little while he can avoid thinking about the event, the smells, and the sounds that seem to lurk behind everything.

The memories themselves feed that sense of danger. When the burnt smell catches him unexpectedly, or when a bus backfires hard enough to sound like an explosion, Lukas is pulled straight back into the convoy scene. Helicopter and aircraft sounds are especially potent; even seeing one pass overhead can leave him tense and scanning the sky. In those moments, the memories do not feel like something he is recalling from the past but like something happening again in the present, and that replay strengthens his conviction that nowhere is truly safe. He is left feeling that he must keep watch, because if he relaxes for even a moment, something terrible could happen. That fear also makes it harder for him to make sense of what happened: the more he replays it, the more the account remains broken apart, and the less able he feels to put it into words.

At the same time, the hours he spends on his phone and gaming have taken on a second function. They keep him from facing the memories directly, but they also seem to preserve the fragments in their raw form; when he finally stops scrolling, the same images rush back with even less order than before. He notices that the more he avoids thinking, the less connected the memory feels, and the more it returns as scattered flashes rather than a coherent narrative. That leaves him feeling cut off from his own life, unsure how to explain what has happened to him and increasingly isolated in it. Over time, the cycle has narrowed his world: he works his bus routes and tries to get through the day, but he is constantly scanning for danger, dreading sudden bangs from traffic, and steering clear of places where crowds or religious gatherings might trap him with his own reactions.

Lukas did not seek help until he began to think, quietly and with growing alarm, that his life might not be worth living anymore. He was frightened by how automatic the avoidance had become and by how little relief it was bringing. He hopes treatment might help him feel less on guard and let him make some sense of the event without being pulled back into it every time he hears a bang, smells something burnt, or catches the sound of helicopters overhead. More than anything, he wants to believe that the world can be something other than a place he has to survive moment by moment.
